conceptBreakdown.content:
A lichen is a composite organism formed by a mutualistic symbiosis between a fungal partner (Mycobiont) and a photosynthetic partner (Phycobiont / Photobiont).

• Partner Roles:
- Phycobiont (Algal/Cyanobacterial Partner): 5–10% of thallus. Photosynthesizes carbohydrates (and fixes atmospheric N2 if cyanobacterial, e.g., *Nostoc*, *Scytonema*).
- Mycobiont (Fungal Partner): >90% of thallus (usually Ascomycete). Provides structural anchorage, absorbs water/minerals, and shields photobiont from UV radiation.

• Morphological Classification:
1. Crustose Lichens: Flat crust tightly adnate to rock/bark (*Graphis*, *Rhizocarpon*). Pioneer species in primary ecological succession.
2. Foliose Lichens: Leaf-like lobed thallus anchored by rhizines (*Parmelia*, *Peltigera*).
3. Fruticose Lichens: Shrubby, branched pendulous structures (*Usnea*, *Cladonia rangiferina*).

• Bio-Indicators of Pollution: Highly sensitive to Sulfur Dioxide (SO2) pollution because SO2 degrades phycobiont chlorophyll. Completely absent in polluted industrial regions.

conceptBreakdown.heading: 8.2 Mycorrhizae
conceptBreakdown.title: 8.2 Mycorrhizae
conceptBreakdown.content:
Symbiotic associations between soil fungi and the roots of higher vascular plants.

1. Ectomycorrhizae: Fungal hyphae envelope the root exterior forming a dense sheath (Mantle) and penetrate intercellular cortical spaces to form an intercellular network called the Hartig Net. Common in forest trees (*Pinus*, *Quercus*, *Eucalyptus*).

2. Endomycorrhizae / Vesicular-Arbuscular Mycorrhizae (VAM): Fungal hyphae do not form an external mantle; instead, they penetrate cortical cell walls (invaginating the plasma membrane) to form branched nutrient-absorbing Arbuscles and storage Vesicles.
- Predominantly formed by zygomycetous soil fungi belonging to the genus *Glomus*.
- Nutritional Benefit: Dramatically enhances plant absorption of insoluble Phosphorus (Phosphate) from soil.
